abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) are widely used to quantify genetic predisposition to complex traits, and their predictive accuracy can be enhanced by incorporating functional annotations into single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) effect-size estimation. Existing approaches typically assume linear relationships between annotations and SNP effects, neglecting predictive aleatoric variance and potential nonlinear regulatory interactions. To evaluate the gains of nonlinear and uncertainty-aware modeling, we developed DeepU-PRS, a deep ensemble framework that extends the linear BLD-LDAK model with a neural network trained on functional annotations to jointly estimate SNP heritability and its aleatoric uncertainty, which are then integrated into a Bayesian PRS model. Across 28 continuous and 8 disease phenotypes in the UK Biobank, DeepU-PRS improved the mean continuous R2 by approximately 10% over linear BLD-LDAK, with the largest gains for traits whose association signals were concentrated, whereas the more diffuse disease traits favored BLD-LDAK. These patterns were reproduced in individual-level data from All of Us. Against a panel of established methods (C + T, Lassosum, PRS-CS, LDpred-funct, and SBayesRC), DeepU-PRS was among the strongest single methods on continuous traits, and ensembles combining DeepU-PRS with the linear baseline and SBayesRC further improved accuracy, indicating complementary predictive signal. These findings highlight the value of modeling nonlinear and uncertain regulatory effects to advance PRS prediction.
